title: The great banquet (Luke 14:15–24)
hook: the invited guests make excuses, so the host fills the hall with the poor and the lame

segments.voice: Yesterday, a widow with no power wore down a judge who feared nobody, just by coming back. Your line was keep knocking. Did you knock on one door again? Day thirty-four.

Jesus is at dinner in the house of a leading Pharisee, and someone at the table says, happily, how blessed will be the one who eats bread in the kingdom of God. Jesus answers with a story about a dinner. A man plans a great supper and invites a lot of people, and they all say yes. The day comes, the food is ready, and he sends his servant out to tell them: come, everything's ready. And one by one, they make excuses. I just bought a field, I have to go and see it. I just bought five pairs of oxen, I have to try them out. I just got married, so I can't come. The hall is set. The food is hot. And every chair is empty.
screen: `A GREAT SUPPER.` → `EVERYONE SAID YES.` → `EVERY CHAIR IS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: Look at those excuses. Some readers think the first listeners laughed out loud. Who buys a field without seeing it? Who buys ten oxen without testing them first? These aren't reasons. They're ways of saying: I have better things to do. And notice what the story shows about how it worked. The guests were invited ahead of time, said yes, and were called again when the meal was ready. They backed out at the last minute, all of them. The host is angry. Then he does something surprising. He tells his servant: "Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in hither the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind." The people who never get invited anywhere. The servant does it and comes back: there's still room. So the host sends him further, out past the town, to the roads and the hedges, where travelers and people with nowhere to go are, and says: "compel them to come in, that my house may be filled." Compel sounds harsh, but think about who's being asked. Someone sleeping by a hedge, told that a rich man wants him at dinner, might well say: that can't be for me. He'd have to be talked into it. A few verses earlier, Jesus tells his own host the same thing plainly: when you give a feast, invite the poor, the maimed, the lame and the blind, the people who can't invite you back. Christians often read the banquet as a picture of the kingdom of God: a table that stays set, where the empty chairs fill with people nobody expected. It's also a story about the ones who were asked first, and chose their fields instead.
screen: `THE EXCUSES ARE A JOKE` · `SAID YES, THEN BACKED OUT` · `THE STREETS AND THE LANES` · `THE HIGHWAYS AND THE HEDGES` · then, large: `THAT MY HOUSE MAY BE FILLED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let some faces come up: people who are rarely invited. The new person at work who eats alone. The neighbor who lost her husband last year. The cousin nobody quite knows what to do with. The friend who always hears about the party afterward. Breathe. Let one face stay. Don't plan a whole evening. Just picture them at your table: a coffee, a walk, a saved seat. Hold that picture. And later today, if you can, make the invitation real. The bell holds the time.
Compel. The host's word to his servant, sent out to bring in the people who'd never believe a feast like this could be for them.
Your line: there's room at the table. Once today, invite someone who's rarely invited, even to something small. A coffee counts. Day thirty-four.

howItsDone: Churches often run community meals, food pantries and open tables where anyone can eat, and some Christians make a point of inviting people who are usually left out.

fork.setup: you're the host. the food is hot, and every guest has sent an excuse. what do you do?
options: send out for the poor, the maimed, the halt and the blind.
fork.reveal: he fills the hall with the people nobody invites, then sends out again, because there's still room.

original.note: Greek: supper, the main meal of the day. Luke's host makes a "great" one.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about rude dinner guests.
what it means: a table that keeps its chairs open for people nobody else invites, and a warning to the ones asked first.
what a scholar hears: "compel them to come in" was later quoted by Augustine to defend using force against a rival church, the Donatists. in the story, it's an urgent welcome.

notes: Review 2026-10-01: 'the first listeners would have laughed' hedged to some readers; 'no respectable host would do' cut; the hedge scene no longer tells the listener what they'd say; practice's 'group chat' image (used on day 25) replaced; 'many Christians/churches' softened.

Luke 14:23 in the KJV begins 'And the lord said unto the servant, Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them...'; the script quotes only 'compel them to come in, that my house may be filled'.
Trapdoor mentions Augustine's use of Luke 14:23 against the Donatists (Letters 93, 185). A Keeper may prefer to leave this out.
The two-stage invitation is drawn from the text itself (bade many, then sent at supper time), not from outside customs.
